newsitem.title: GERMANY: Pilots, instruments blamed for Dominican crash.
newsitem.headline: Pilots, instruments blamed for Dominican crash.

text.p: The final report into the crash of a Boeing 757 airliner off the Dominican Republic last February blames pilot error linked to faulty instruments for the disaster, German television reported on Sunday.

The Boeing 757 was leased to the Dominican national airline Alas Nacionales by Turkish carrier Birgenair and was heading for Frankfurt and Berlin. It plunged into the sea soon after taking off from the Dominican resort of Puerto Plata on February 6, killing all 189 people aboard, most of them German tourists.
The crash report by the Dominican Republic's civil aviation authority is due for official release on November 1.
But the Sat1 television station said one of its reporters had been invited to Santo Domingo last Friday and received the report directly from chief investigator Emanuel Souffront.
Preliminary investigations had already pointed in March to the failure of an airspeed indicator which led the pilots to believe, wrongly, that they were travelling too fast.

The ascent which they started eventually slowed the aircraft below a critical speed. They failed to respond to a dramatic "stick-shaker" warning which caused the steering column to vibrate, so that the aircraft stalled and plunged into the Caribbean.
"The probable cause of the accident was the failure on the part of the flight crew to recognise the activation of the stick-shaker" and their failure to act to prevent a stall, the report said.
"Before the stick-shaker warning, there was confusion among the crew due to erroneous indications of an increase in relative velocity and a warning of excessive velocity," it added.

The report said the crew realised some of the airspeed indicators were faulty but failed to make use of several back-up indicators or switch to an alternative data source which could have given them a correct reading.
It said the Turkish crew became confused as a result of poor knowledge of the aircraft's instrumentation systems. But it also noted that such an eventuality was not part of their standard training.

It recommended that Boeing should build an extra warning device into the cockpit to point to discrepancies in the airspeed readings, and include procedures for verifying airspeed in its operating manual. It called for pilots to be trained to cope with such a situation.
The report found that an exterior pressure tube or "pitot tube" had probably contributed to the accident by giving a faulty reading because it was blocked by dirt or insect remains.

It said there had been a failure to cover the tube while aircraft was on the ground, or to follow the recommended procedure by checking that the tube worked after the plane had been on the ground for some time -- in this case 20 days.
"The investigators concluded that the blocked pitot tube was not the probable cause of the accident but that it was a contributing factor," the report said.
